catalog_quote: This work is based on the Copperbelt dialect.[fn.2] Like the majority of languages in this volume, Bemba is a tone language that does not have stress or any kind of accent marking. [...] [Sec. 2, prepub p.2:] Bemba contrasts two level tones, high and low, which are generally phonologically treated as H vs. Ø following basic Bantu language assumptions (Kisseberth & Odden 2003). This means that phonologically low tones are not active and surface low-toned forms are considered to be lexically toneless but surface as low-toned if they are not affected by High tone spreading rules. [...] Vowels in Bemba can be short or long with the mora as the tone-bearing unit.[fn.4] [...] [Sec. 3, prepub p.10:] Finally, although there is no penultimate lengthening in Bemba, there appears to be some lengthening of the final syllable in both the initial subject and the final constituent in the declarative sentence. We have not carried out systematic durational comparisons but notice it here and in figures discussed below. [...] [Philippson 1991, p.485:] e) langues dans lesquelles la pénultième ne semble jouer aucun rôle, quel qu'il soit : ganda; bukusu; nyamwezi; bemba, tonga; kikuyu. [p.487:] Au stade II, l'assimilation proximale a abouti à la neutralisation de l'opposition HH/HB, sans que soit encore atteint un vrai système accentuel; c'est le cas des langues de Tanzanie Occidentale : nyamwezi et sukuma, ainsi que du bemba.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Bemba (bemb1257) is not in the catalog. works with stress in the title: (1)-(2) Hyman 1995 JALL 16:3-39 (two Glottolog records for the same paper) -- a prosodic-morphology (circumscription/minimality) analysis of perfective imbrication, not a stress source; no open copy exists (OpenAlex/S2 closed, De Gruyter bot-walled, absent from Hyman's Berkeley site); low priority. (3) Philippson 1991 Doctorat d'Etat thesis -- theses.fr marks it inaccessible and it is not on HAL, but the author's full PDF (542 pp., text layer) is on his DDL-Lyon page and is now. Bemba is one of its well-described sample languages and is explicitly classed as a tone language in which the penult plays no role and no true accentual system has emerged (pp. 91-92, 465, 485, 487). This corroborates the already-held deciding statement Kula & Hamann 2017 p. 1 ('Bemba is a tone language that does not have stress or any kind of accent marking'; no penultimate lengthening, p. 10), which I re-read from disk. Hyman 2013 (penultimate lengthening in Bantu) was checked and does not mention Bemba. no word stress (tone language).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bemba is described as a two-tone (H vs. toneless/L) language with contrastive vowel length and no word stress or accent of any kind; unlike many Eastern/Southern Bantu languages it also lacks phrase-penultimate lengthening (only an unquantified utterance-final-syllable lengthening is noted).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; the source denies any stress/accent system.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The authors note possible (unmeasured) lengthening of the final syllable of the initial subject and of the sentence-final constituent in declaratives, explicitly not penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the language's prosodic system in general (word and phrase): no lexical stress, no accent, no penultimate-lengthening prominence at phrase level. Based on Copperbelt Bemba (Ndola) speakers; authors note tonal (not stress) differences between Copperbelt and Northern Bemba.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (and the JIPA Illustration) describe Copperbelt Bemba (Ndola speakers), an urban variety of bemb1257; Glottolog's Bemba (Zambia) bemb1257 covers both Northern ('standard', Kasama) and Copperbelt Bemba, which the authors say differ in tone-spreading rules but not (per their statement) in having stress. Distinct from Bembe/Beembe (bemb1255, beem1239) and from Town Bemba as a contact variety.

new_statements.reading: Bemba has no word stress and no accent of any kind; it is a pure two-tone (H/L, mora-TBU) language, without penultimate lengthening. Independently corroborated by the newly obtained Philippson 1991 thesis (author's PDF from DDL Lyon), which lists Bemba among the East African Bantu languages 'dans lesquelles la pénultième ne semble jouer aucun rôle, quel qu'il soit' (p. 485) and classes it as tonal, not having reached 'un vrai système accentuel' (p. 487; also p. 465 and pp. 91-92). If a catalog record is created, code Bemba as a tone language with no word stress (Copperbelt variety; Philippson's data are largely from Sharman/Meeussen and informants, i.e. Northern/standard Bemba as well).

sources.quote: p. 485: "e) langues dans lesquelles la pénultième ne semble jouer aucun rôle, quel qu'il soit : ganda; bukusu ; nyamwezi ; bemba, tonga ; kikuyu." -- p. 487: "Au stade II, l'assimilation proximale a abouti à la neutralisation de l'opposition HH/HB, sans que soit encore atteint un vrai système accentuel; c'est le cas des langues de Tanzanie Occidentale : nyamwezi et sukuma, ainsi que du bemba." [Translation: (e) languages in which the penult seems to play no role whatsoever: Ganda; Bukusu; Nyamwezi; Bemba, Tonga; Kikuyu. / At stage II, proximal assimilation has led to the neutralization of the HH/HB opposition, without a true accentual system having yet been reached; this is the case of the Western Tanzanian languages Nyamwezi and Sukuma, and of Bemba.]
sources.locator: Ch. 6 sec. 3.5.2 (e), p. 485; also Ch. 6 sec. 3.6.1 p. 487, Ch. 6 sec. 3.2.4.1 p. 465, Ch. 4 sec. 2.3 'Le cas du bemba' pp. 91-92 (running page numbers = PDF page numbers; the TOC/index pagination is ~7 pp. off)
sources.note: Bemba (group XI, M42, one of the '++' well-described languages, pp. 71-72) is treated as a tone language with mora-counting tone association and four tonal patterns in disyllables (pp. 91-92: umúlilo, umúpení, úmucélé, úmucéka). In the typological/diachronic synthesis it is explicitly placed among languages where the penultimate plays no role at all (p. 485) and at 'stade II', i.e. tonal, not yet a true accentual system (p. 487; also p. 465: neutralized HH/HB in nominal themes 'mais n'en sont pas pour autant passées à un système accentuel'). No word stress / no penultimate accent.
